stories.headline: U.S. stocks hit a record as investors bet companies will make even fatter profits
stories.dek: The S&P 500 rose 0.6% to 7,818.93, its first record since August, even with oil near $100 and bond yields above 5%.
stories.caveman: On Tuesday the S&P 500, the big list of 500 U.S. companies that sits inside many retirement accounts, climbed 0.6% to 7,818.93. That beat its old all-time high from August. It is now up 23% since its low point in late March. The Nasdaq also closed at a record, 27,599.79, and the Dow rose 253 points to 51,521.28. Why are stocks so happy when so much looks bad? Oil is expensive because of the war with Iran, prices are rising fast, and borrowing costs are high. The answer is profits. Analysts at FactSet expect S&P 500 companies to report earnings per share almost 30% higher than a year ago. Frozen-fry maker Lamb Weston jumped 7.5% after beating forecasts. Constellation Energy jumped 12.2% after a long-term deal to sell Google about as much power as a new nuclear reactor makes. The 10-year Treasury yield slipped to 5.28% from 5.31%, and Brent oil settled at $100.58.
stories.why_it_matters: Record stock prices make people with 401(k)s feel richer, even while many Americans feel squeezed by the cost of living. But the whole rally leans on one thing: companies keep delivering big profits. Earnings season starts this week with Delta on Friday and big banks next week.
stories.camps: Bulls: Strategists at Barclays say strong profits are letting stocks "win the tug-of-war against yields." Nvidia is up 28.3% this year, about double the market, as AI spending keeps growing. Worried side: AP notes that much depends on companies actually hitting those high expectations; if they miss, prices could fall fast. Some critics also warn of a bubble in AI stocks, and high bond yields make stocks look less attractive than safe bonds.
stories.image_alt: A trader works on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange.

terms.explain: An index tracking 500 big U.S. companies; the most-watched measure of the U.S. stock market.
A U.S. stock index full of tech companies.
A company's profit divided by its number of shares. Investors use it to judge growth.
The interest the U.S. government pays to borrow money. Higher yields make loans pricier for everyone.
The international benchmark price for oil.
A common U.S. workplace retirement account, often invested in stocks.

stories.headline: Paramount closes its $81 billion takeover of Warner Bros., creating one Hollywood giant called Skydance
stories.dek: HBO Max, CNN, CBS, "Harry Potter" and "Top Gun" now sit under billionaire David Ellison, a Trump ally.
stories.caveman: It's done. On Tuesday, Skydance-owned Paramount finished buying Warner Bros. Discovery for $81 billion, or nearly $111 billion counting debt. The new company is simply called Skydance. That puts two of America's oldest movie studios under one roof, along with HBO Max, Paramount+, CBS and the news channel CNN. David Ellison runs it with new co-CEO Ynon Kreiz. The fight took about a year. Warner first picked Netflix, but Netflix walked away after Paramount raised its offer to $31 a share. Twelve Democratic state attorneys general sued to block the deal, then settled in September; the company promised more U.S. filmmaking, money for laid-off workers, and a new "News Editorial Independence Board" for CNN and CBS. To pay for it, Paramount took big money from Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates. The FCC allowed those funds to own up to 100% of the company indirectly, with no voting rights.
stories.why_it_matters: Fewer, bigger companies now decide which movies get made, what streams, and how a major news network is run. CNN is especially in the spotlight because President Trump has attacked it for years and has close ties to the Ellison family.
stories.camps: Supporters: Ellison called it "a historic day" and has repeated his commitment to making movies; director James Cameron backed him, and Trump called it a "great" merger. Critics: thousands of Hollywood workers, including Jane Fonda and Mark Ruffalo, signed a letter warning of fewer jobs and less choice. The FCC's only Democratic commissioner, Anna Gomez, called the foreign-money approval alarming. Ellison says CNN will stay independent and is keeping Mark Thompson as its editor-in-chief, but critics point to turmoil at CBS under Skydance.
stories.image_alt: The Paramount Pictures water tower in Los Angeles with the Hollywood sign in the distance.

terms.explain: When two companies combine into one.
An offer to buy a company that goes around its own leaders, straight to shareholders.
A state's top lawyer, who can sue companies to protect consumers.
Federal Communications Commission, the U.S. agency that oversees TV, radio and phone networks.
Laws meant to stop companies from getting so big they crush competition.
The idea that owners should not tell journalists what to report.

stories.headline: After angry protests, Spain rushes out 21 emergency housing measures before its snap election
stories.dek: An 87-year-old woman's eviction set off nationwide marches; the plan includes a €10 billion fund for first-home loans.
stories.caveman: Spain has a housing crisis: rents and home prices have shot up, and many people can't afford a place to live. Last month, 87-year-old María del Carmen Abascal was evicted from her Madrid home. Her story set off protests all over the country, and on Monday night police and protesters clashed in Barcelona. On Tuesday, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's government approved 21 urgent measures. They include longer eviction protections for vulnerable people, rules for renting single rooms, a new tax on seasonal rentals, a ban on speculative property buying, and tax breaks for owners and tenants who pay on time. The government will also set up a €10 billion fund to lend up to €50,000 to people buying their first home. Parliament had voted down similar steps last week, which is why Sánchez called an early election for Nov. 29. Because Parliament is dissolved, a smaller stand-in body of 69 lawmakers must approve the plan; his coalition needs 35 votes.
stories.why_it_matters: Housing costs are squeezing young people in many rich countries, from Spain to Taiwan. Spain is now testing whether fast government action can calm public anger, and whether housing can decide a national election.
stories.camps: Sánchez's side: "We will not allow any more evictions like the one Maricarmen suffered," he said, pushing the measures as proof he is acting. Opposition side: right-wing parties voted down his earlier emergency decrees, and critics see the timing as a campaign move. Some economists also argue that rent rules and new taxes can scare off landlords and builders, while supporters say only strong rules protect renters.
stories.image_alt: Tens of thousands march over Spain's housing situation in Barcelona on Oct. 5, 2026.

terms.explain: When a tenant is legally forced out of their home.
An election called earlier than scheduled.
Two or more parties governing together because none has a majority alone.
Short-term rentals, like vacation apartments for tourists.
A rule issued directly by the government that later needs lawmakers' approval.

stories.headline: Southeast Asia's power needs are growing faster than its answers, the IEA warns
stories.dek: Demand for electricity per person rose almost 30% in 10 years, and the Iran war has exposed how fragile the region's energy supply is.
stories.caveman: The International Energy Agency, a group that tracks the world's energy, released a report on Tuesday about Southeast Asia, which includes countries like Vietnam, Thailand, Indonesia and the Philippines. Its message: these fast-growing countries need much more electricity, for air conditioning, data centers and factories, but risks to their supply are piling up faster than solutions. Energy use per person in the region rose almost 30% over the last 10 years. The IEA expects demand to keep growing about 5.4% a year until 2030. The Iran war and the closing of the Strait of Hormuz caused fuel shortages and higher prices there. Unlike Japan and South Korea, most of these countries have small energy reserves. Some burned more coal and bought Russian oil to get by, but some also signed nuclear deals, paid people to install solar panels and gave rewards for buying electric cars. The IEA says neighbors should share electricity and get power from more sources.
stories.why_it_matters: Southeast Asia is a major factory hub and a growing market for Taiwan's companies. If its power is unreliable or expensive, that hits supply chains, prices and climate goals around the world.
stories.camps: IEA view: head Fatih Birol calls the region one of the world's most dynamic, but says its energy needs face an uncertain global landscape. Hopeful view: Amy Kong of Zero Carbon Analytics says the war gave governments "a bit of a reality check" that could push cleaner power. Doubtful view: analysts warn that border fights between neighbors and very different national energy markets may block power-sharing. Putra Adhiguna of the Energy Shift Institute says the region needs "much more drastic change."
stories.image_alt: A solar installer secures a panel onto the roof of a home in Manila, Philippines.

terms.explain: International Energy Agency, a Paris-based group that studies and advises on world energy.
A narrow sea passage near Iran that a big share of the world's oil normally sails through.
Having enough reliable, affordable energy even when something goes wrong.
A building full of computers that run websites and AI; it uses huge amounts of power.
To spread out across many sources so one problem can't knock you out.

stories.headline: Hackers stole personal data on 1.3 million people from Arizona's court system after one bad email click
stories.dek: The stolen files include records on unpaid fines, about 30,000 protection orders and 150,000 foster-care reports.
stories.caveman: Arizona's Supreme Court says a cyberattack on the state court system copied personal information about 1.3 million people. Officials think it began when a court employee clicked a dangerous link in an email. The stolen data covers people who owe court fees, fines or repayments for traffic and criminal cases, going back as far as 30 years. The attackers also took records on nearly 30,000 protection orders, which are court orders to keep someone away from a victim, and 150,000 reports since 2010 from a foster-care board that advises on cases where parents may be unable to care for a child. Court tech staff spotted the attack on a backup server on Sept. 24 and shut it down about two hours later. The court has been notifying people. No records were changed or deleted, and data on jurors, witnesses and court workers was not taken.
stories.why_it_matters: Protection-order and foster-care files can reveal where vulnerable people live or very private family details. This shows how one click can expose sensitive government data, and why phishing training matters.
stories.camps: The court's side: spokesperson Alberto Rodriguez said, "We don't have any evidence it has been used or shared," and that no court cases were delayed. The worry: investigators still don't know who did it, and once data is copied it can surface later.
stories.image_alt: A man enters the Arizona Supreme Court building in Phoenix.

terms.explain: An attempt to break into computers to steal, change or destroy data.
A fake email or message that tricks you into clicking a bad link or giving up a password.
A court order telling someone to stay away from another person, often in abuse cases.
A system where children live with other families when their parents can't safely care for them.
A computer that stores copies of data in case the main system fails.

stories.headline: McDonald's is sued over an AI pricing tool, accused of helping franchise owners fix prices
stories.dek: The lawsuit says the tool shares secret store-level data among competing restaurants; McDonald's says "AI does not set menu prices."
stories.caveman: Most McDonald's restaurants in the U.S. are owned by local business people called franchisees: they own 95% of the chain's 14,000 U.S. stores. McDonald's gives them an AI-powered tool that recommends menu prices based on a store's sales, location and rivals' prices. A new federal lawsuit, filed Friday in Illinois for a customer named Michael Thomas of DeKalb, says that tool breaks competition law. It claims the tool gathers private data, like store-level sales, that competing restaurants would never normally share, and that this pushed prices up. The suit calls it "algorithmic price-fixing aimed at customers who are already stretched thin." Thomas says he noticed different prices at McDonald's stores near his home. McDonald's says the lawsuit is "filled with inaccuracies" and that the tools are optional and "do not automate, coordinate or fix pricing in any way." The suit wants to become a class action.
stories.why_it_matters: More and more companies, from landlords to retailers, use software to set prices. Courts are now deciding whether sharing data through an algorithm can be the same illegal price-fixing as rivals secretly agreeing on prices in a back room.
stories.camps: The customer's side: McDonald's has "significant leverage over its franchisees" and can pressure them to follow its price suggestions. McDonald's side: "AI does not set menu prices at McDonald's restaurants - McDonald's franchisees do." It points out that franchisees don't always follow its advice; CEO Chris Kempczinski said in August that only 60% of U.S. restaurants were offering its proposed menu of 10 items under $3. A judge will now decide whether the case can go forward.
stories.image_alt: McDonald's Golden Arches signs in Los Angeles.

terms.explain: A local owner who pays a big brand to run a store under its name.
When competitors agree on prices instead of competing; it's illegal in the U.S.
A set of computer rules that turns data into a decision or suggestion.
A lawsuit where one or a few people sue on behalf of a large group with the same complaint.
Laws that protect competition and stop companies from ganging up on customers.

stories.headline: RFK Jr. says AI will free Americans from "medical tyranny." Doctors and some MAHA allies push back
stories.dek: At a summit sponsored by OpenAI, Anthropic and others, the health secretary praised AI; critics called the event "pay-to-play."
stories.caveman: Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is the U.S. health secretary and leader of the "Make America Healthy Again," or MAHA, movement. He built fans by warning about big drug, vaccine and food companies. Last week, at an invite-only MAHA summit with AI and Silicon Valley executives, he cheered for a new industry: artificial intelligence. He said AI would free Americans from "medical tyranny" by letting them "fact check their own medical advice," so they would never again be told to just "trust the experts." OpenAI and Anthropic, which both offer health chatbots, were among the sponsors. Sponsors paid up to $300,000, and many got speaking slots next to top health officials. Doctors say his idea misunderstands AI: these tools are trained on medical research, so what they give you is mostly the same expert advice. Even some MAHA figures say the movement is cozying up to the corporations it once attacked.
stories.why_it_matters: Millions of people already ask chatbots about their health. Whether the government treats AI as a replacement for doctors or a helper for them will shape medical care, privacy of health data, and how much big tech gets to do with little oversight.
stories.camps: Kennedy's side: HHS spokesperson Emily Hilliard says AI will help people "understand" and "interrogate" their own health data with their doctors and give doctors more time with patients. Medical experts: Dr. Zeke Emanuel says "He obviously doesn't understand how AI works"; Dr. Robert Wachter at UCSF agrees AI can empower patients, but says it will mostly spread the best science, not contrarian views. MAHA critics: vaccine researcher Dr. Robert Malone called the summit "classic pay-to-play." Organizer Tony Lyons says they are simply "trying to build the biggest movement we can."
stories.image_alt: Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. arrives to speak in Dallas.

terms.explain: "Make America Healthy Again," the health movement led by Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
Department of Health and Human Services, the U.S. federal health agency.
An AI program you talk to by typing or speaking.
When money buys access to powerful officials or a seat at the table.
An expert on the right and wrong of medical and science choices.

stories.headline: Brooklyn startup Reflection AI releases Beam, an open-weight model meant to rival China's best
stories.dek: The company says Beam matches leading Chinese open models on reasoning tests while using 3 to 4 times less computing power; that claim isn't verified yet.
stories.caveman: Some AI companies keep their models closed, so you can only use them through their apps. Others release "open-weight" models that anyone can download and run. Right now many of the most popular open models come from China, like DeepSeek, Qwen and Z.ai. Reflection AI, a two-year-old startup in Brooklyn, New York, wants to change that. On Monday it unveiled Beam, its first big model. Beam has 501 billion parameters, but only 23 billion work on each task, which makes it cheaper to run. It learned from 23.8 trillion tokens of text and can read about 1 million tokens at once. Reflection says Beam scores about the same as Z.ai's GLM-5.2 on hard reasoning tests while using "3-4x less inference compute." The company has raised about $4.7 billion from backers including Nvidia and Sequoia, at a $25 billion valuation, and signed more than $7 billion in deals with SpaceX and Nebius for chips. It says it will release Beam's weights this month.
stories.why_it_matters: Who builds the world's open AI models matters: companies and governments that run open models depend on whoever trained them. The U.S. has worried that China is winning this part of the AI race.
stories.camps: Reflection's side: it calls Beam a "workhorse model" and wants to sell "AI factories" so banks, firms and countries can train private versions on their own data; it is already testing this with South Korea's Shinsegae Group. Caution: TechCrunch notes the performance claims haven't been independently checked, and Beam handles only text, while rival U.S. open model Inkling from Thinking Machines Lab also handles images. Nvidia, an investor, also benefits because these systems run on its chips.
stories.image_alt: Reflection AI's Beam announcement graphic.

terms.explain: An AI model whose trained settings are released so anyone can download and run it.
The internal numbers an AI model learns; more usually means bigger and more capable.
A design where only part of a big model switches on for each task, saving computing power.
Small chunks of text, like pieces of words, that AI reads and writes.
When a trained AI model is actually used to answer questions.
How much investors say a company is worth.

stories.headline: Over 250,000 rally across France for school funding as police fire tear gas at teen protesters
stories.dek: Nearly 500 people were detained Tuesday; more than 6,500 arrests in two weeks, mostly of minors, have become an election issue.
stories.caveman: In France, high school students have been protesting since mid-September. They say their schools are falling apart: classrooms without enough desks or chairs, no air conditioning, rats in some buildings, and too few staff. On Tuesday, the government says 266,000 people marched across the country, including 56,000 in Paris, to back them. Police fired tear gas in Paris and other cities, and nearly 500 people were detained. Over two weeks of school blockades, police have made more than 6,500 arrests, mostly of minors. On Monday a 15-year-old boy lost a hand in an incident involving a police stun grenade. The interior minister says 715 officers have been hurt. Classes were fully or partly stopped at 891 schools. Anger is also about fuel prices driven up by the Iran war, tight budgets and rising inequality, as France heads toward a presidential election to replace Emmanuel Macron.
stories.why_it_matters: It shows how fast a student movement can grow into a national crisis, and it raises a hard question for any democracy: how should police handle protests by teenagers?
stories.camps: Government: Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez says the police response was proportionate in "almost all cases" and that some protests turned into riots. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu says students must be heard, but denounced "ultra violence" and called claims of police racism a "lie," while promising to investigate any "accidents." Protesters and the left: far-left lawmaker Aurélien Le Coq calls the violence "absolutely unbearable"; a university student said it makes no sense "to hit minors"; parents say demonstrating is a legitimate right.
stories.image_alt: A protester kicks a tear gas canister during scuffles after a school-funding demonstration in Paris on Oct. 6, 2026.

terms.explain: A chemical spray that stings eyes and throat; police use it to break up crowds.
Blocking the entrance to a place, like students blocking their school's gates.
A device that makes a loud bang and bright flash to scare and scatter crowds.
The French government department in charge of police and public safety.
The French word for high school.

stories.headline: Three years after Oct. 7, much of the world sees tragedy in Gaza. Many Israelis still see only a threat
stories.dek: AP visited the Israeli towns attacked by Hamas in 2023 and found deep trauma, little public talk about Gaza's civilians, and an angry election ahead.
stories.caveman: On Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led militants attacked southern Israel, killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostages. Israel's war in Gaza followed. Over 74,000 Palestinians have been killed, according to Gaza's Health Ministry, and most of Gaza's 2 million people now live in tent camps or in rubble, a year after a fragile ceasefire. Israel's military controls more than 60% of Gaza. This is the first anniversary with all hostages out of Gaza, alive or dead. AP reporters went to Sderot, an Israeli town right next to Gaza. From a lookout, Israelis peer through binoculars at the ruined Gaza town of Beit Hanoun. Memorials line the highway where people were shot while fleeing. Israeli media report little about Gaza's Palestinians, and journalists still can't freely enter Gaza. A new Israeli documentary, "NAZA," in which military insiders describe what they called the systemic killing of civilians, caused outrage at the filmmakers rather than the government. Israel also faces its first election since the attack.
stories.why_it_matters: Today is the anniversary. Understanding why many Israelis and much of the world see the same war so differently helps explain why peace is so hard and why the coming Israeli election matters.
stories.camps: Israeli survivors: Ziporah Livneh says "We are post-traumatic, all of us," and that the answer is to respond strongly to evil while not building a country on revenge. Some Israelis say there are no real civilians in Gaza because Hamas is everywhere; some Palestinians say the same about Israelis because most serve in the army. Critics inside Israel: Amit Gurfinkel, who wants an official inquiry into the security failures, worries about Israel's reputation; Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has long resisted such an inquiry. Global view: there is widespread shock over how Israel has fought the war, and the International Criminal Court has issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu.
stories.image_alt: Visitors gather on a hill overlooking the Gaza Strip in Sderot, southern Israel.

terms.explain: The Palestinian militant group that ruled Gaza and led the Oct. 7, 2023 attack.
A person taken and held by force, often to pressure others.
An agreement to stop fighting, which may be temporary.
An Israeli town right next to the Gaza border.
An official investigation into what went wrong.
A court in The Hague that tries people accused of war crimes.

stories.headline: U.S. military locks down troops in Okinawa for two days after a Marine is arrested in a woman's killing
stories.dek: Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, is accused of strangling a 39-year-old woman in a Naha hotel; he has denied it, Japanese media report.
stories.caveman: Okinawa is a Japanese island that hosts a huge American military presence: about 80,000 Americans, nearly 30,000 of them active-duty troops. Last weekend, Okinawa police arrested Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, a 20-year-old Marine from Ohio stationed at Futenma Air Station. Police suspect he strangled Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in the capital, Naha, early Saturday and stole her wallet and backpack. Security cameras showed a man entering the hotel with her and leaving alone. He has denied the allegations, according to Japanese media. On Tuesday, the top U.S. Marine commander there, Lt. Gen. Benjamin Watson, ordered a 48-hour pause from Wednesday to Friday: troops are restricted from leaving base and must take training on discipline and their duties to the community. "Their home is our home," he wrote. Police say crimes linked to the U.S. military rose to 101 cases last year from about 40 in 2020.
stories.why_it_matters: Okinawa is close to Taiwan, and U.S. forces there are a key part of plans to deter China. Every crime by U.S. troops weakens local trust and can make it harder for Japan's government to expand military cooperation.
stories.camps: U.S. military: Watson says trust with Okinawans is essential to the alliance and "when that trust is damaged, it affects the strength of our alliance." Okinawa residents: many have long opposed the bases, and anger is rising again; one resident told the Okinawa Times that "discipline and troop education are not working at all." Others on the island have come to see the bases' value because of China. Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi wants closer military work with the U.S., which this case could make harder.
stories.image_alt: U.S. MV-22 Osprey aircraft parked at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in Ginowan, Okinawa.

terms.explain: A chain of Japanese islands southwest of mainland Japan, home to most U.S. bases in Japan.
A member of the U.S. Marine Corps, a branch of the U.S. military.
A U.S. Marine air base in the middle of a crowded Okinawan city.
To discourage an enemy from attacking by showing strength.
A formal promise between countries to help defend each other.

stories.headline: Germany arrests a former spy chief, 80, on suspicion of treason and selling state secrets
stories.dek: Prosecutors say August Hanning, who ran the BND foreign intelligence agency from 1998 to 2005, got about 2,000 documents from an old aide.
stories.caveman: The BND is Germany's foreign spy agency, like the CIA in the U.S. On Tuesday police arrested August Hanning, 80, who led it from 1998 to 2005. Prosecutors say he is "strongly suspected" of treasonous espionage and spying out state secrets. They also arrested a former aide, named only as Manfred D. under German privacy rules. He had been Hanning's chief of staff and later worked for several BND bosses until 2026. Prosecutors say the two agreed in 2010 that the aide would keep sending secrets to Hanning for money. Over the years he allegedly passed about 2,000 documents, many classified. Hanning is suspected of using the information in private consulting and sharing some with people working for foreign spy agencies. Officials have not said which countries. The case grew out of a separate investigation into the 2024 kidnapping of a Hamburg businesswoman's children in a custody fight.
stories.why_it_matters: Spy agencies run on trust. If a former chief really sold secrets, it would damage Germany's standing with allies who share intelligence, and it raises questions about what retired officials do after they leave.
stories.camps: Prosecutors: they say there is strong suspicion but have not named the foreign services involved; Hanning has not been convicted, and the AP report did not include a response from him. Lawmakers: Green Party member Konstantin von Notz, who sits on the committee overseeing spy agencies, called the story "deeply troubling" and wants former officials with top security clearances banned from private consulting. The BND did not immediately comment.
stories.image_alt: August Hanning, former president of Germany's BND, at a Bundestag hearing in 2015.

terms.explain: Germany's Federal Intelligence Service, which spies abroad.
Betraying your own country, for example by helping a foreign power.
Spying: secretly gathering information for another side.
Secret government information that only approved people may see.
Official permission to see secret information.

stories.headline: National Book Award fiction finalists: Danticat and Luiselli are in, Marlon James is out
stories.dek: Edwidge Danticat is now a three-time finalist; debut novelist Morgan Thomas made the cut, while Booker finalist "The Disappearers" was snubbed.
stories.caveman: The National Book Awards are one of the biggest prizes for American books. On Tuesday the National Book Foundation named five finalists in each of five categories. Who's hot in fiction: Edwidge Danticat's "Dèy," about a woman who witnesses a mass shooting in a Miami mall; Valeria Luiselli's "Beginning Middle End," a family story across generations and continents; Hannah Lillith Assadi's "Paradiso 17," following an exiled Palestinian around the world; Julián Delgado Lopera's "Pretend You're Dead and I Carry You," set in Colombia; and debut novelist Morgan Thomas's "Mad Eden," about a transgender healthcare worker in Florida. Who's not: Marlon James's "The Disappearers," about a brutal attack on gay men in 1980s Jamaica. It was a Booker Prize finalist and had made this prize's longlist of 10. Winners get $10,000 at a dinner in Manhattan on Nov. 18. Salman Rushdie and Perri Klass will get honorary medals.
stories.why_it_matters: Award lists shape what bookstores push and what readers pick up. This year's fiction list leans into gender identity, gun violence, exile and migration, the arguments America is having right now.
stories.camps: Fans of the list: NPR points out that Danticat, a finalist in 1995 and 2007, now gets a third shot, and that a debut novelist is in the running. Critics of the list: the James omission stands out because The New York Times praised "The Disappearers" as one of the century's best. Some readers also argue prize lists lean toward political themes; others say that's what serious fiction is doing today.
stories.image_alt: Book covers of "Dèy" by Edwidge Danticat and "Beginning Middle End" by Valeria Luiselli.

terms.explain: Major yearly U.S. book prizes run by the National Book Foundation.
One of the last few books still in the running for a prize.
The bigger first list of nominees, before it's cut down to finalists.
An author's first published novel.
A top British prize for novels written in English.

stories.headline: Beyond fiction: Gaza, prisons and queer parenthood fill the rest of the National Book Award finalist lists
stories.dek: Two Gaza books made the cut, in poetry and in translation; Norway's Karl Ove Knausgaard is up for the translated prize.
stories.caveman: The National Book Awards also have prizes for nonfiction, poetry, translated books and young people's literature. Nonfiction: Colin Asher's "The Midnight Special," a secret prison history of American music; Abdelrahman ElGendy's "Huna," a memoir of revolution and prison in Egypt; Camonghne Felix's "Let the Poets Govern"; Sara Nović's "Mother Tongue"; and Joseph Osmundson's "Spawning Season: An Experiment in Queer Parenthood." Poetry: Victoria Chang, Carolina Ebeid, Brenda Hillman, Susan Stewart, and Fady Joudah's "Exhibit G: Poems, Essays, and Photographs of Gaza." Translated literature: Karl Ove Knausgaard's "The School of Night," Vicente Luis Mora, Intan Paramaditha, Mohamed Mbougar Sarr, and Samar Yazbek's "Your Presence Is a Danger to Your Life: Voices of Survival and Witness in Gaza." Young people's literature: Elana K. Arnold, Tae Keller, Keala Kendall, Julian Randall, and David Levithan with Gabriel Duckels for "The Fight of Our Lives: AIDS in America."
stories.why_it_matters: These lists often decide which books libraries and schools buy. Two Gaza books and books about prison and queer families show which stories the literary world wants the public to hear right now.
stories.camps: Supporters: the lists give space to voices often left out, such as prisoners, queer parents and Palestinians in Gaza, and to writing from Indonesia, Senegal and Spain in translation. Skeptics: some readers feel awards juries reward timely politics over craft, and books about Gaza in particular split American readers. Winners will be named Nov. 18.
stories.image_alt: A collage of 2026 National Book Award finalist book covers.

terms.explain: Writing about real people and events, like memoirs and history.
A true story an author writes about their own life.
Books first written in another language and translated into English.
Books written for kids and teens.
An umbrella word for people who are not straight or not cisgender.

stories.headline: Nobel Literature Prize is Thursday: is this the year for an American like Jamaica Kincaid or Thomas Pynchon?
stories.dek: Critics float Antiguan-American writer Kincaid and China's Can Xue; only 18 of 122 literature laureates have been women.
stories.caveman: The Swedish Academy will announce the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature on Thursday, Oct. 8, at 11:00 GMT, which is 7 p.m. in Taipei. The winner gets about $1.2 million. Nobody outside the academy knows who will win, but critics and bookmakers love to guess. An AFP preview names Jamaica Kincaid, 77, the Antiguan-American author of the 1990 novel "Lucy," as a serious contender. American novelist Thomas Pynchon is one of the "usual suspects" who comes up every year. Betting site lists, reported by Lit Hub, put Chinese experimental writer Can Xue near the top. Swedish critics quoted by AFP also mention Argentina's Samanta Schweblin. Only 18 of the 122 literature laureates so far have been women. Last year's prize went to Hungary's László Krasznahorkai.
stories.why_it_matters: The Nobel can turn a writer into a global name overnight and sends readers back to their books. An American win would be the first since Louise Glück in 2020.
stories.camps: Optimists: critics say it may be time for more women and writers from outside Europe, and Kincaid fits both. Skeptics: the academy famously surprises everyone, and favorites often lose; Lit Hub jokes that "nobody knows anything." Some readers also argue betting odds tell you more about hype than about the judges.
stories.image_alt: A Nobel Prize medal.

terms.explain: A yearly prize from the Swedish Academy for a writer's whole body of work.
The group in Stockholm that picks the literature Nobel.
Someone who has won a major prize.
Companies that take bets and set odds on events.
Someone with a real chance to win.

stories.headline: In a new memoir, GOP Sen. Thom Tillis calls his Hegseth vote the "biggest regret of my career"
stories.dek: "How to Lose Friends and Antagonize Presidents" says at least 30 Republican senators privately doubt Trump and predicts a midterm "bloodbath."
stories.caveman: Thom Tillis is a Republican senator from North Carolina who is leaving office soon after clashing with President Trump. His new book, "How to Lose Friends and Antagonize Presidents," came out Tuesday. In it, he says his deciding vote to confirm Pete Hegseth as defense secretary in January 2025 is the "biggest regret of my career," and that he "should've stopped" Robert F. Kennedy Jr. from becoming health secretary. He writes that at least 30 GOP colleagues have privately "expressed reservations" about Trump's actions, but praise him in front of cameras. He criticizes tariffs, aggressive immigration raids and the Iran war, and predicts a "bloodbath" for Republicans in November's midterms. Still, he mostly spares Trump himself: "my beef is not with him, but the idiots he's got working for him," and he calls Trump "an amazing political talent." Trump earlier called Tillis a "QUITTER!" online.
stories.why_it_matters: It's a rare inside look at how senators weigh fear for their careers against their own doubts. It also lands weeks before the midterm elections that will decide who controls Congress.
stories.camps: Tillis's view: he says he didn't want to be the lone vote blocking Trump's picks, and that opposing Trump on everything means you "lose all influence." Critics might say: speaking out after you've decided not to run again costs little; AP notes he joins a long list of Republicans who got louder once they had less to lose. Trump's side: he has attacked Tillis as a quitter, and Hegseth has denied the allegations Tillis says worried him.
stories.image_alt: Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., arrives for a hearing on Capitol Hill.

terms.explain: A true story an author writes about their own life.
When the Senate votes to approve a president's pick for a top job.
Nickname for the Republican Party, "Grand Old Party."

Taxes on imported goods.

stories.headline: Kenya confirms its first Ebola case and death, as the world's fastest-growing outbreak spreads
stories.dek: A Kenyan man who lived in Congo flew home from Uganda; health workers are tracing 28 contacts plus 23 fellow passengers and four crew.
stories.caveman: Ebola is a deadly virus that spreads through contact with an infected person's body fluids, like blood or vomit, or things they touched. A big outbreak began in eastern Congo and was declared in mid-May. It now has at least 8,400 cases and more than 4,000 deaths, making it the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history. On Tuesday, Kenya said a Kenyan citizen who had lived in Congo for seven years became its first confirmed case and first death. He got sick about a month ago, traveled by road to Kampala, Uganda, and flew to Nairobi on Saturday. His family took him to Nairobi Hospital, where he was isolated, tested positive, and died late Monday. Officials found 28 contacts, including family and health workers, and are tracing 23 passengers and four crew from his flight. Contacts must isolate for 21 days. Kenya is the fourth country with a case in this outbreak, after Congo, Uganda and France.
stories.why_it_matters: Ebola reaching a major travel hub like Nairobi raises the risk of wider spread. Fast testing, tracing and protective gear make the difference between one case and many.
stories.camps: Health officials: the Africa CDC praised Kenya's "rapid identification, isolation and testing," and WHO delivered about 1,000 Ebola tests and 1,000 protective kits. On the ground: Doctors Without Borders says fighting the outbreak in Congo "is like fighting a megafire" because many hot spots flare at once, and responders face attacks, misinformation and rebel violence. WHO warns it could become deadlier than the 2014-2016 West Africa outbreak that killed more than 11,000 people.
stories.image_alt: Kenya Health Minister Aden Duale announces Kenya's first Ebola case in Nairobi on Oct. 6, 2026.

terms.explain: A rare, often deadly virus that causes fever and bleeding.
A sudden rise in cases of a disease in one area.
Finding everyone a sick person was near, so they can be checked and isolated.
Keeping a sick or exposed person away from others.
World Health Organization, the United Nations' health agency.
Personal protective equipment, like gloves, masks and gowns.

stories.headline: Army study found shock gloves bought by ICE cause intense pain and fear; critics say safety isn't proven
stories.dek: ICE knew about the findings before signing a $16.7 million deal for 6,000 pairs, records obtained by a watchdog show.
stories.caveman: ICE is the U.S. immigration agency that arrests and deports people. In August it signed a $16.7 million contract for 6,000 pairs of electric shock gloves, which give a painful jolt when an officer touches someone's skin. A watchdog group, American Oversight, got records through a lawsuit and shared them with AP. They include a never-before-released Army study from October 2024 at the military prison at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. Army staff pretended to be fighting prisoners. After being shocked, they stopped resisting within seconds and felt "fatigue, soreness and excessive apprehensiveness to being shocked again." Some said just seeing the glove made them want to obey. The study says the shock overloads nerve endings in the skin to cause pain, and wet or oily skin made it worse. ICE leaders knew about the study before buying. The maker, Compliant Technologies, must deliver within six months.
stories.why_it_matters: These gloves could be used on detainees and protesters. A weapon that causes intense pain but leaves no mark raises big questions about abuse and accountability.
stories.camps: ICE's side: it calls them "distraction and de-escalation devices," safer than other non-lethal tools, and says fast compliance keeps officers safe and prevents deadly force; it says "officers are highly trained in de-escalation tactics." Critics: American Oversight's Chioma Chukwu says the study shows the gloves cause intense pain but "does not establish that they are safe." Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto and 15 other Democratic senators asked ICE in August to drop the plan or explain it, and say ICE hasn't answered. Border czar Tom Homan says it could "be awhile" before the gloves are used.
stories.image_alt: A Kentucky jailer shows an electric shock glove used at his facility.

terms.explain: Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the U.S. agency that arrests and deports immigrants.
An organization that monitors the government and exposes problems.
Meant to stop someone without killing them, like a Taser or pepper spray.
Calming a tense situation so it doesn't turn violent.
A U.S. law that lets the public request government records.

stories.headline: Zambia will sign a $3.6 billion health deal with the U.S. only after cutting patient-data clauses
stories.dek: The health minister says Zambia "will not be obliged to share any specimen"; other African nations agreed to hand over data within five days.
stories.caveman: After the Trump administration shut down USAID, once the world's biggest aid donor, the U.S. started signing one-on-one health deals with African countries under its "America First" approach. The idea: the U.S. slowly gives less money while the countries spend more of their own. But some deals asked countries to share patients' health data and samples, like blood, with the U.S. government. Zambia pushed back. On Tuesday, Health Minister Roma Chilengi said Zambia will sign a revised five-year deal worth $3.6 billion in combined money, with the U.S. giving $1.5 billion, and that clauses on sharing individual health data have been "completely removed." Signing is set for Thursday. The U.S. has signed deals with about two dozen African nations since last year. At least nine agreed to send data and specimens within five days of a request, and the U.S. can pass them to up to 10 unnamed non-government groups to develop tests and treatments.
stories.why_it_matters: Health data and blood samples are valuable for making medicines. Who controls them, and whether poorer countries get fair benefits, is a big question in global health.
stories.camps: Zambia's view: Chilengi called the U.S. a critical partner and said Zambia is grateful, but would not give up its people's data. U.S. approach: the administration says countries should take more responsibility for their own health systems, and data and samples help develop diagnostics and treatments. Critics: data-sharing rules with unnamed private groups have been some of the most controversial parts of the deals, raising privacy and fairness worries.
stories.image_alt: Zambia's Foreign Minister Mulambo Hamakuni Haimbe speaks at the U.N. General Assembly.

terms.explain: The U.S. Agency for International Development, the foreign aid agency the Trump administration dismantled.
A deal between two countries.
A sample, like blood, taken from a patient for testing.
One part or rule in a contract.

stories.headline: After the far right's big win in an eastern German state, migrants ask whether they still belong
stories.dek: AfD fell three seats short of a majority in Saxony-Anhalt; a Syrian doctor wonders about going back, while a pharmacist vows to stay.
stories.caveman: The Alternative for Germany, or AfD, is a far-right party that wants fewer immigrants and faster deportations. On Sept. 6 it won its best result ever in Saxony-Anhalt, a state in former East Germany, falling three seats short of a majority in the 83-seat state legislature. On Tuesday the new legislature met for the first time and chose AfD's Tobias Rausch as speaker. Ola Akhras, a doctor who fled Syria in 2018, says she and her husband talk every day about going back. She feels valued at work but has faced hostility while shopping and no longer feels safe going out at night. "Our children will never be recognized as Germans here," she said. Pharmacist Mohamad Aldabagh, who came in 2015, says he has rebuilt his life and won't let anyone take it away. Migrant counseling centers say their phones are ringing off the hook. As of August, 27.1% of hospital doctors in the state did not have German citizenship.
stories.why_it_matters: A decade after Germany welcomed over a million refugees, a far-right party could lead a state government for the first time since World War II. That would affect the people who now help run its hospitals and pharmacies.
stories.camps: AfD and its voters: they blame migrants for problems like slow growth, high inflation and energy costs, and want stricter selection of foreign workers, refusing those they call "culturally foreign." Migrants and experts: professor Rahim Hajji asks how an aging state with labor shortages will find skilled workers if it shrinks the pool it's willing to recruit. Aldabagh says, "We are needed. We are not the black sheep in this country." It is still unclear whether AfD can form a government; the next governor likely won't be chosen before December.
stories.image_alt: AfD supporters wave party and German flags at a demonstration in Berlin.

terms.explain: Alternative for Germany, a far-right, anti-immigration political party.
Political groups on the extreme right, often strongly nationalist and anti-immigrant.
A state in eastern Germany; its capital is Magdeburg.
Forcing someone to leave a country.
People with training for jobs like doctor, nurse or engineer.
